analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and its health care and education companion law.
analysis.headline: H.R. 6515, a full repeal of the Affordable Care Act with 7 cosponsors, died in committee without a vote in the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Affordable Care Act and the 2010 reconciliation law that fixed parts of it, effective October 2022, and restore the law as it stood before. That would end the ACA's protections for people with preexisting conditions, its premium subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and the guarantee that young adults can stay on a parent's plan. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the main gainers would be high-income taxpayers, since the ACA's surtax on investment income and other financing taxes would disappear, and insurers and providers that sell outside ACA rules, since plans could again turn away or charge more to people with preexisting conditions. States that opposed Medicaid expansion would no longer face it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners and insurers outside ACA rules

how_it_helps.text: Repealing the ACA removes the 3.8% net investment income tax that falls mainly on high-income households, one of the law's main funding sources.
It would remove all ACA rules, allowing insurers to return to pre-2010 practices such as medical underwriting and lifetime limits.

analysis.who_pays: The people who would bear the cost are the tens of millions who get coverage or protections through the ACA: subsidized marketplace enrollees, adults added to Medicaid through expansion, people with preexisting conditions who would again be uninsurable or priced out, young adults on parents' plans, and seniors who benefit from ACA-related drug savings. Also colleges, since the same law ended the government's student loan middleman business and reinvested the savings in aid, which would be undone too.
analysis.who_pays_short: Marketplace enrollees, Medicaid adults, people with preexisting conditions

drawbacks.text: Repeal would strip consumer protections including the ban on denying coverage for preexisting conditions, annual and lifetime benefit limits, and the requirement that plans cover essential health benefits.
Premium subsidies and Medicaid expansion, which together cover tens of millions of people, would end, and no replacement program is included in the bill.
The bill also repeals the health and education provisions of the 2010 reconciliation act, rolling back changes to the federal student loan system made by that law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers tax relief to high-income households and freedom from federal health rules, but its costs fall on the sick, the poor, and the uninsured — the groups least able to buy their own coverage. It contains no replacement for the coverage and protections it removes. Any honest weighing has to note that the loss of protections and subsidies is large and concentrated on people with health needs, while the tax gains accrue mainly to high earners.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to eight House committees and a health subcommittee and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs introduced the bill on January 28, 2022, with Reps. Chip Roy and Thomas Massie joining as original cosponsors.
Six Republicans cosponsored the bill in total; no Democrats did.
The bill was referred to eight committees and, at the subcommittee level, to the Health and Indigenous Peoples subcommittees, where it sat without action.
No hearing, markup, or vote is recorded for the bill before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: the ACA's subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and consumer protections stayed in place for the rest of the Congress. Nothing changed for anyone; the bill's absence of support among all but a handful of Republicans made its outcome a foregone conclusion.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The millions who kept ACA coverage and protections

for.name: Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it.

for.name: Chip Roy and Thomas Massie
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.role: Majority control of the House and its committees
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or floor vote across eight committees.

against.name: House Republican conference (all but 7)
against.what_they_did: Did not cosponsor the bill, leaving it with no path to the floor even under their own party's leadership in future sessions.

sides.party_line_note: All 7 supporters were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored it, and the Democratic majority buried it in committee.

industries.note: Repeal would free insurers from ACA rules such as guaranteed issue and essential benefits, letting them return to pre-2010 practices like denying or pricing out people with preexisting conditions. Some individual-market insurers that rely on ACA subsidies would lose customers.
Repeal removes the 3.8% net investment income tax, a large tax cut concentrated among high earners.

The 2010 reconciliation law ended bank-based federal student lending; repeal restores the pre-2010 system, reopening space for private lenders to originate federal loans. This reverses a consolidation of student aid through the government.
Hospitals would lose reimbursements tied to Medicaid expansion and marketplace coverage, though some providers outside ACA networks could gain flexibility.
